sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does each heading name what its section holds?** No. The one heading, "About the trust" (about x 180–474, y 120–165), covers the first half of the paragraph: what the trust looks after, its 1987 founding, its staff and members. From about y 406 to 536 ("Work days run every second Saturday… cutting back gorse"), the text turns into an invitation to volunteer, and no heading names it. A reader who scans headings sees only background and skips the one part that asks them to do something. The heading itself is descriptive, so this is not a WCAG 2.4.6 failure as such. It is a structure problem: two topics share one label. Split the paragraph at "Work days run…" and give the second part its own heading that says what it offers, e.g. "Join a work day". Defect (common sense, in the spirit of WCAG 2.4.6). Weight: major if the page is meant to recruit volunteers, as the copy suggests.
2. **The invitation can't be acted on** (copy; no checklist line, raised under "The words are part of the design"). "Work days run every second Saturday, and anyone is welcome to join for the morning" (y ≈ 406–439) gives no time, no meeting place, no next date and no way to sign up or ask. "Every second Saturday" can mean every other Saturday or the second Saturday of each month. That is a commitment line the viewer acts on, so the two readings can send someone out on the wrong day. A willing reader has to go and find the details somewhere else, and many won't. Give the next date, the start time, the meeting point and one exact action, e.g. "Next work day: Sat 6 Dec, 9am at the quarry car park. Just turn up, or email to say you're coming." Defect. Weight: major.
3. **The voice changes partway through** (copy; no checklist line). The paragraph calls the trust "it" up to "Today it has four staff…" and then says "We provide tools, gloves…" (y ≈ 439). The reader feels the switch from a third-person report to a direct invitation, and the welcoming part gets less weight than it could. Pick one voice; "we" suits a volunteer appeal better. Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The type is kept to two levels, a bold heading and regular body text at what looks like 20 px, one dark neutral on white. It reads as quiet and trustworthy, which suits a small charity, and nothing on the page is decoration. The copy is concrete: eleven miles, two woods, 1987, four staff, about ninety volunteers, just over two thousand members. Those specifics make it sound like this trust and nobody else, so keep them when revising.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each heading names what its section holds)

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies. The image is a 1280×800 text section with a heading and one paragraph.

**Findings**
None.

The checklist has no line for one hierarchy problem, so I'm passing it on for you to place. The invitation to volunteer is the only thing on the page that asks the reader to do something. It sits in the middle of the paragraph, at about y≈405–535: "Work days run every second Saturday, and anyone is welcome to join for the morning…". It has the same size, weight and colour as the history before it. A reader skimming the page gets the heading and the first lines about history and never sees the ask. You could file this as taste or common sense, since no checklist entry covers it. The fix is to give the volunteering part its own paragraph or subheading so the ask has a place in the order of importance. It may belong under arrangement or text instead.

**What's working.**
- **One clear entry point.** The heading "About the trust" (x≈180–474, y≈122–165) is clearly the largest and boldest thing on the page. It looks about 1.8 times the body size and is set in a heavy weight, so the eye lands there first.
- **Clean contrast between the two levels.** The heading differs from the body in size and weight, and it looks a little darker too. There is no in-between size to confuse the two levels.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** and **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** All the content sits in one column from x≈180 to x≈800. The right ≈480 px (x≈800–1280) and the bottom ≈250 px (y≈550–800) are empty. The empty space is in one place, but nothing on the page gives it a job. The left margin (≈180 px) is much smaller than the right void (≈480 px), and nothing on the right balances the dark heading and dense paragraph. The page tips left and looks like something failed to load, such as a photo of the moor, a sidebar, or a "join a work day" panel. It doesn't look like a chosen asymmetric layout. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance") says a heavy side needs a counterweight, and Tschichold and Müller-Brockmann count large unexplained empty areas as a fault. Fix direction: either give the right side something with weight (a picture of the paths or woods, or the work-day details pulled out as a small panel), or treat the column as a deliberate reading measure by centering it or widening the left margin so the empty space looks chosen. If an image is meant to sit there, check that it actually renders. Defect (unbalanced, unfinished look), convention (Arnheim). Weight: major. It doesn't stop anyone reading, but it makes the page look broken or unfinished, which costs a small trust its credibility.
2. **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion, such as halves, thirds, or the golden section, rather than arbitrary splits?** The horizontal splits are roughly 180 / 620 / 480 px, and the vertical ones roughly 120 px above the heading and 250 px below the text. None of these follow halves, thirds, or any other ratio, so the column looks placed by default rather than set in the frame. Fix direction: settle the column and margins on one simple ratio, which will usually come out of fixing finding 1. The source calls this a soft guide, so this is taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Heading and body share one exact left edge at x≈180, and the space between them (≈35 px) is only slightly more than the line pitch (≈32 px). The heading clearly belongs to its text, and the block reads as one calm unit. Keep that tight heading-to-body spacing in any revision.
- The reading column is narrow enough to set a comfortable measure, so the paragraph reads easily even though it's one long block. Keep the column width if you fill the right side.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty right side is a missing image or panel (a load or capture problem) or the actual design. Check this in a live browser. Also how the column behaves at narrower widths, where the imbalance may disappear.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (empty space gathered and deliberate; visual weight balances; main divisions follow one proportion)

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is long text broken up by headings, short paragraphs, or lists?** No. The whole body copy is one 11-line block (x≈180–800, y≈200–550), and it covers two different topics. Lines 1–6 tell the trust's history and size. Then "Work days run every second Saturday…" (line 7, y≈406) changes to an invitation to the reader: anyone is welcome, tools, gloves and a hot drink are provided, no experience is needed, and here is the kind of work. That invitation is the only part a visitor can act on. It starts mid-line, straight after "…a few miles of the moor.", so anyone skimming sees one grey block and never finds the offer. Nielsen ("How Users Read on the Web") says web readers skim and skip dense unbroken blocks. The fix: split at "Work days run…" into a second paragraph. The invitation could also get its own short heading or lead line (for example, when and how to join), so the one actionable thing on the page can be found without reading all of it. Defect. Weight: major. On an "About" page for a volunteer trust, the call to volunteer is likely the point, and here it is buried.

**What's working.**
- The paragraph is set well for reading. Lines run about 55–62 characters at roughly 20 px with generous leading (about 1.6), and the rag is soft with no runt on the last line ("…across the path."). Long copy is comfortable to read here.
- One sans family is used in two clearly different weights: a bold heading of about 44 px over regular body text. The two levels are plainly distinct, and the near-black on white is well above 4.5:1.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (long text broken up by headings, short paragraphs, or lists)

**Walk (Color).** All dark neutral on white, with no hue anywhere.
- Small palette: yes
- Saturated colour kept to a small share: yes
- Clear range of light and dark: yes
- Warm forward, cool back: yes
- Matching colours look the same: yes
- No vibrating edges: yes
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes
- Colour never the only signal: yes
- Dark theme not pure black: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so I didn't need to open any reference entries.

**Section.** Color: applies, though the page has almost no colour. It's near-black type on a white field with no hue at all.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Contrast:** The heading and body (around x 180–800, y 120–550) are a dark charcoal, not pure black, on white. That gives strong contrast for easy reading without the harsh glare of pure black on white. The structure is fully clear in grayscale.
- **Restraint:** With no accent colour, nothing competes with the heading. For a short "About" text block, that's the right call. If the page later gets a link or a call to action, there's room for one accent hue to own it.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The image has no photo, illustration, icon, logo or mark. It is only a heading ("About the trust") and one paragraph of text.

**Findings**
None.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The text column runs from about x 180 to 800 px. Everything to its right, about x 800 to 1280 px from top to bottom, is empty white. That could be the intended layout, or it could be a picture that never loaded. A missing picture usually leaves a broken-image icon or an outlined box, and there is neither here. Open the page in a live browser to see whether an image (for example, a photo of the moor or of a work day) is meant to sit in that space.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped
